title: Organisational AI Adoption Survey
intro: This questionnaire should be completed by the most senior person in your organisation who can name the specific systems in use: typically the CIO, IT director, or head of digital transformation. It takes about 22 minutes. Every participating organisation receives a confidential benchmarking report comparing its results with its sector.

questions.text: Consent to participate
Name of organisation
questions.help: Used only to prevent duplicate entries and to send your benchmark report. Never published.

questions.text: Which best describes your organisation?

options.label: Federal government ministry, agency or authority
Regional / city administration bureau or office
Hospital, health centre or health agency
Startup or software / IT services company
NGO, civil society or development partner

questions.text: Your role

options.label: CEO / Director General / Head of institution
CIO / IT Director / Head of Digital

questions.text: How confident are you that you can accurately describe the technology systems currently in use across your organisation?
questions.help: There is no wrong answer. This helps us weight responses appropriately.

options.label: Very confident, I have full visibility
Confident for my department, less so for others
Limited, I would need to ask colleagues

questions.text: Does your organisation hold a national or regional mandate for AI, digital or technology policy, regulation, coordination or funding?
questions.help: For example: authoring policy, issuing licences, setting standards, funding programmes, or coordinating other institutions.

options.label: No: we deliver services or operate, we do not set policy

questions.note: Routes the policy module. Asked rather than inferred from the organisation name, because a list of which bodies hold a mandate would go out of date the first time one is merged or renamed -- which in this sector happens often.

questions.text: Where is your head office?
In which regions do you have operations or branches?
Number of employees
questions.note: Each band carries its numeric bounds so that cross-field checks can use them (see `constraints`). Without them a rule comparing headcount to a band would have to parse the label, which breaks the first time a label is reworded.

questions.text: Approximately how many staff work in IT, data or technology roles?
Year the organisation was established
Does your organisation have any foreign ownership, parent company or formal technology partnership abroad?
Can your organisation access foreign currency to pay for international software or cloud services?
questions.help: This is one of the factors we are testing as a predictor of AI adoption.

options.label: Yes, but with delays or limits

questions.text: Approximate annual operating budget (ETB)
Legal registration status in Ethiopia

options.label: Registered both in Ethiopia and abroad

questions.text: What stage is your main product or service at?
questions.help: Commercial maturity of what you offer, distinct from the AI-specific maturity asked about later.

questions.text: Which market sector(s) does your organisation operate in? Choose all that apply.
questions.help: Different from the organisation type above: a bank's AI work might sit in fintech AND health, for instance.

questions.text: Is at least one founder or senior leader a woman?

sections.title: Digital baseline
sections.help: Before asking about AI we need to understand the digital substrate it would sit on.

questions.text: Which of the following does your organisation currently have? Tick all that apply.

options.label: A management information system (HR, finance or operations)
A central database of core records
APIs that let other systems read our data
Services that citizens or customers use digitally end-to-end

questions.text: What proportion of your organisation's core records are stored digitally rather than on paper?
How would you describe your internet connectivity at your main site?
How often does an electricity interruption stop work at your main site?
Do you have backup power sufficient to keep servers running?
Is there a written digital transformation or ICT strategy for your organisation?

sections.title: Understanding of AI: definition gate
sections.help: This short section establishes a shared definition so that later answers are comparable. It is not a test.

questions.text: In this survey, 'artificial intelligence' means software that learns patterns from data to make predictions, classifications, recommendations, or to generate text, speech or images, for example machine learning models, speech recognition, computer vision, or large language models such as ChatGPT. It does NOT mean ordinary automation, rules-based workflows, dashboards, or standard database software, even when these are described as 'smart' or 'intelligent'.
Based on that definition, which of these would you count as AI? Tick all that you consider AI.

options.label: A model that predicts next month's demand from past sales data
A dashboard showing this month's figures against last month's
A system that converts spoken Amharic into text
A workflow that automatically emails a reminder when a form is overdue
A chatbot that answers customer questions in natural language
A barcode scanner that looks up a product code
Software that flags suspicious patterns in transaction data

questions.text: How would you rate the general level of understanding of AI among senior leadership in your organisation?
And among technical staff?

sections.title: Kinds of AI technology in use
sections.help: Adoption status (section D) says how deeply AI is embedded. This says WHAT KIND of AI it actually is -- a chatbot, a spreadsheet formula labelled 'AI', and a fraud-detection model are very different technologies, and 'adopting AI' hides that difference completely.

questions.text: Which of these kinds of AI technology does your organisation use, pilot, or plan to use within a year? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Predictive analytics or machine learning on your own data
Language technology for Amharic or another Ethiopian language
AI agents that take actions on their own (booking, filing, replying)

questions.note: Independent of the maturity ladder in section D on purpose. A national picture built only from 'adopted: yes/no' cannot say whether the country is running chatbots or running fraud models, and those imply completely different skills, risks and policy responses. Kept out of D so the two lenses -- how deep, and of what kind -- can be cross-tabulated rather than conflated into one number.

questions.text: Of those, which would you say are genuinely reliable in production today, not just working in a demonstration?
questions.note: The gap between AT1 and AT2 is a second, technology-specific over-claiming measure, parallel to the maturity self-versus-computed gap in section D.

questions.text: Has your organisation ever used, trialled or deployed any AI system as defined above?
What are the main reasons your organisation has not adopted AI? Choose up to three.
Is your organisation planning to start using AI in the next 24 months?
Which level best describes your organisation today? (self-assessment)
questions.help: We will also compute an independent score from your later answers. Both are recorded.

options.label: 0. Unaware: AI is not relevant to our work
1. Aware / exploring: discussed or trained, no pilot yet
2. Piloting: at least one trial, not in production
3. Deployed: at least one AI system in real production use in one area
4. Scaled: AI in production across two or more areas, with a budget line
5. Core: AI is embedded in how we deliver our core services

questions.text: Which of the following has your organisation ACTUALLY done? Tick only what has already happened, not what is planned.
questions.help: Your maturity score is computed from this list.

options.label: We have assessed where AI could be useful, in writing
We have run at least one pilot with real data
At least one AI system is in production use today
That system has a named internal owner
There is a budget line for AI in the current fiscal year
We monitor a deployed model's accuracy in production over time
We have retrained or fine-tuned a model on our own data
AI systems run in two or more different departments
We have a written data-sharing agreement with another organisation
We have an internal policy or guideline on responsible AI use
We have carried out a bias or fairness check on a deployed system
Withdrawing our AI systems would materially disrupt service delivery
We use autonomous self-optimising quantum inference for scheduling

questions.text: Please name each AI system currently in production use. Add one row per system.
questions.help: This is the evidence check. If a system cannot be named, it is not counted as deployed.

options.label: Off-the-shelf international service (e.g. ChatGPT, Azure, Google)
Provided by a donor or partner project

fields.label: Month and year it went live
Roughly how many people use it
Which languages does it work in?

questions.text: How many AI pilots has your organisation started in total?
questions.note: With D7b this gives the pilot-to-production conversion rate: a key reported indicator and the clearest single measure of whether pilots translate into service.

questions.text: And how many of those reached production use?
For pilots that did NOT reach production, what stopped them? Choose up to three.

options.label: The data was not good enough
We lacked the skills to maintain it
It did not deliver enough value
It could not get internal or regulatory approval
Foreign currency was not available to continue

questions.text: Who initiated AI adoption in your organisation?

options.label: A donor or partner proposed it

questions.text: Has your organisation measured the results of any AI system against a baseline?
If you have measured results, what changed? Please give the actual figures if you can.
Are staff using AI tools that the organisation has not approved?

options.label: We have no way of knowing

questions.note: Benchmark item. Globally about one organisation in five cannot answer this at all (AvePoint 2026); the 'no way of knowing' share is the finding, not the residual.

questions.text: Has any AI deployment been delayed by concerns about data security, data quality or governance?
questions.note: Benchmark item. Globally nearly nine in ten organisations report such a delay, averaging about six months (AvePoint 2026).

questions.text: In the last twelve months, has any AI system been involved in a data-security or privacy incident?
questions.note: Benchmark item. Pairs with I-section confidence questions to reproduce the global confidence-incident paradox: high stated confidence alongside widespread incidents.

questions.text: Does your organisation use AI systems that take actions on their own (booking, filing, replying, approving), rather than only producing text or predictions?
questions.note: Agentic AI. Asked of everyone, not only current adopters, because the global pattern is adoption outrunning the governance that should precede it.

questions.text: How confident are you that your organisation could prevent unauthorised access to the data its AI systems can reach?
questions.note: Benchmark item, paired with D14. Globally more than four organisations in five report confidence here while 62-72% of those same organisations report an AI-related unauthorised-access incident (AvePoint 2026). Asking both is what makes the contradiction measurable rather than rhetorical.

sections.title: Technical depth: building or adopting?
sections.help: This section separates using AI from building it. Both are legitimate; they are different national capabilities and are counted separately.

questions.text: Which best describes the DEEPEST technical work your organisation has done with AI?
questions.help: Your own view. A separate score is computed from the next question; both are recorded.

options.label: 1. Consume: we use AI products as supplied, without changing them
2. Configure: we integrate and tailor AI (prompts, our own documents, APIs), but do not change the model itself
3. Adapt: we have fine-tuned or retrained an existing model on our own data
4. Produce: we have trained a model from scratch or developed a new method

questions.text: Which of these has your organisation ACTUALLY done? Tick only what has already happened.
questions.help: Your technical depth score is computed from this list.

options.label: Used an off-the-shelf AI product or service
Integrated an AI service into a workflow or system through an API
Built a system that answers from our own documents or data (retrieval)
Fine-tuned or retrained an existing model on our own data
Trained or fine-tuned a model on Ethiopian-language data
Published or open-sourced a model, dataset or tool
Ported a model to run on low-power or offline devices

questions.text: What data did you train or fine-tune on?

options.label: Our own administrative or operational records
Our own images, audio or video
Data we collected or had annotated for the purpose

questions.note: Distinguishes genuine domestic model development from fine-tuning on imported data. Feeds the adopt-adapt-produce analysis.

questions.text: Where do the AI systems you use actually run?

options.label: Entirely on a vendor's service; we send data out and get answers back

questions.note: Where inference runs determines who holds the data and who can be cut off. A sector at high adoption but entirely vendor-hosted has bought a service, not built a capability.

questions.text: If a model you rely on started giving wrong answers, could your own staff diagnose and fix it?

options.label: Partly, we could diagnose but would need help to fix
No, we would depend entirely on the supplier
We would not know it was wrong

questions.note: The sharpest single measure of real versus purchased capability, and the one most likely to separate sectors that look similar on adoption alone.

questions.text: Has your organisation contributed anything back to the wider AI community: a dataset, model, tool, standard or publication?
For each area, indicate your organisation's current status.

row_options.label: Customer or citizen service (chatbots, call centres)
AI used BY teaching staff (lesson prep, grading)
AI used BY students (tutoring, homework help)

questions.text: Where would AI create the MOST value for your organisation in the next three years? Choose up to three.
Describe the single biggest operational problem in your organisation that you believe AI could help solve.
questions.help: Answers here feed directly into the national use-case portfolio in the white paper.

questions.text: Is that problem currently solvable with the data you already hold?

options.label: Yes, the data exists and is usable
The data exists but is not usable (paper, scattered, poor quality)

questions.text: Which general-purpose AI tools are used by staff in your organisation, whether officially or unofficially?
Does your organisation have a policy governing staff use of such tools?

options.label: No, but we are aware staff use them

questions.note: Shadow AI use vs governance gap is a reported finding.

sections.title: Ethical use in sensitive areas
sections.help: About decisions that affect a person's health, money, liberty or access to services -- the uses where a wrong or biased output causes real harm, not merely inconvenience.

questions.text: For each of these, what oversight exists before an AI-assisted decision takes effect?
questions.note: The same five-point shape as the sector use-case matrices, so ethical oversight can be read against deployment status rather than reported as a free-standing opinion. A system in production (section D) with 'no review process' here is the headline risk finding this module exists to surface.

questions.text: Does your organisation have a written policy or guideline on the ethical use of AI?

options.label: Yes, and staff are trained on it
No, but we follow informal norms

questions.text: Which of these safeguards are actually in place, in any of your AI systems?

options.label: Testing for bias or unfair outcomes across groups
A human in the loop for high-stakes decisions
A specific, understandable explanation given when a decision goes against someone (not just 'declined')
Telling the person affected that an AI system was involved
A route for someone to appeal or contest a decision
Limiting what personal data the system can see

questions.text: Should Ethiopian law require a human to review a high-stakes automated decision (credit, hiring, benefits, policing) before it takes effect?

options.label: Yes, for the highest-stakes cases only
No, this would slow things down for no real benefit

questions.text: Optional: describe the most ethically difficult AI-related decision your organisation has faced, and how it was resolved.

sections.title: Health sector module
sections.help: Sector-specific items. Every sector module follows the same shape so that sectors remain comparable.

questions.text: Does your facility or agency operate an electronic medical record (EMR) system?
questions.note: The binding constraint on Ethiopian health AI. Roughly 70 facilities have an EMR against ~30,000 reporting into DHIS2, and aggregate DHIS2 data cannot train or run patient-level models.

questions.text: How does your facility report into DHIS2?

options.label: Directly from our own digital system
Staff enter it into DHIS2 by hand
On paper, aggregated at woreda level
We do not report into DHIS2

questions.text: Have you, or has any clinician at your facility, personally used an AI tool as part of a real patient's diagnosis or treatment (not a demo, training, or conference)?
For each clinical area, what is your current status?

row_options.label: Guidance assistant for health extension workers

questions.text: For any AI tool used in clinical care: has it been validated on ETHIOPIAN patient data?

options.label: Yes, validated on Ethiopian patient data
Validated elsewhere, not on Ethiopian data
No validation that we know of
We use no clinical AI tool

questions.note: The central safety question. Published Ethiopian evaluations exist as research studies but none has been traced to a routine clinical deployment; this item measures the gap directly.

questions.text: Do you hold Ethiopian Food and Drug Authority authorisation for any software or AI used as a medical device?

options.label: No, and we believe it is required
No, and we did not know it applied
Not applicable, we use no such device

questions.note: EFDA issued a Software-as-a-Medical-Device and AI guideline in 2022, ahead of most African regulators. Whether anything has actually been authorised through it is the open question.

questions.text: How many FULL-TIME radiologists and pathologists are on your staff (not visiting or part-time)?
questions.note: Specialist scarcity is what makes diagnostic AI valuable here; pairing it with YH3 shows whether AI is being deployed where the scarcity actually is.

sections.title: Financial sector module
sections.help: Sector-specific items. Every sector module follows the same shape so that sectors remain comparable.

questions.text: For each area, what is your current status?
Is any customer-facing decision made FULLY automatically, with no person reviewing it?

options.label: Yes, but only approvals: declines are reviewed
No, a person reviews every decision

questions.note: Ethiopia has no algorithmic-transparency or liability rule, so fully automated declines are being made with no statutory basis for contesting them. Pairs with CIT D3 on whether citizens would know how to complain.

questions.text: What data feeds those decisions?
questions.note: Alternative-data scoring emerged in Ethiopia largely because the credit bureau is not open for referencing. This records what is substituting for it.

questions.text: Which model-risk controls are in place? Tick all that apply.

options.label: A documented inventory of models in production
Independent validation, separate from the team that built the model
A defined action trigger when performance degrades
A documented override and appeal route, with override rates logged
Testing for different outcomes by gender, region, or lack of formal credit history
A board-approved AI or model-risk policy

questions.note: The governance items a financial regulator would ask for. The NBE has issued no model-risk guidance, so this measures what institutions do in its absence.

questions.text: Where is customer data used for model training and scoring held?
questions.note: Proclamation 1321/2024 and the 2025 NBE licensing directive require domestic storage of customer data, which constrains use of foreign public cloud. This measures actual compliance.

questions.text: Did you build your scoring or fraud models in-house, or does a vendor supply them?

options.label: Built with a vendor, maintained in-house
Entirely vendor-operated, we see only the output

questions.note: Concentration check: if most institutions answer 'entirely vendor-operated' and name the same supplier, sector-wide model risk is correlated and invisible to any single institution.

sections.title: Agriculture sector module
sections.help: For agricultural research institutes, agri-businesses and cooperatives. Every sector module follows the same shape so that sectors remain comparable.

questions.text: For each area, what is your current status?

row_options.label: Index insurance or agricultural credit scoring

questions.text: Through which channels do your services actually reach farmers?

options.label: The 8028 hotline or another IVR line
We do not reach farmers directly

questions.note: With roughly 76% of the population rural and internet penetration near 21%, the delivery surface is extension agents and IVR, not apps. This measures whether AI outputs travel on channels farmers actually have.

questions.text: In how many languages is your advisory content available?
questions.note: The national farmer hotline reaches five languages out of eighty-plus. Quantifies the exclusion directly in the sector where most Ethiopians work.

questions.text: Do you hold machine-readable, georeferenced datasets (soil, plots, yields, weather, imagery)?

options.label: Yes, and we share them externally

questions.text: Has any AI system you deploy been independently evaluated for accuracy or impact?

options.label: Yes, and the results are public

questions.note: Ethiopian agricultural AI pilots are widely announced and rarely evaluated. The share answering 'no' against the share reporting production systems in YA1 is a headline finding.

questions.text: How is your AI or digital work funded, and when does the current funding end?

options.label: Donor project funding ending within two years
Donor project funding ending within one year

questions.note: Donor-cycle dependency is the mechanism by which agricultural pilots die. Measured rather than assumed.

sections.title: Industry sector module
sections.help: Function ladders follow the World Bank Firm-level Adoption of Technology design, so results are comparable with the 2022 Ethiopian FAT baseline and with other countries.

questions.text: For each business function, which best describes the MOST ADVANCED method you use?
questions.help: Answer for the method actually in use, not one you are trialling.
questions.note: The FAT extensive/intensive-margin design. The 2022 Ethiopian FAT survey found 0.0% of firms using big-data analytics or AI and an average function sophistication of 1.3 (small) to 1.8 (large); this item measures movement against that baseline.

questions.text: Do your production machines produce digital data (sensor readings, counts, downtime logs)?

options.label: Yes, captured automatically into a system
Some machines produce data we do not capture

questions.note: Without machine data there is nothing for industrial AI to learn from. This is the sector's equivalent of the EMR question in health: the precondition, not the application.

questions.text: How is equipment maintenance decided?

options.label: Based on inspection or condition readings
A model predicts when to intervene

questions.text: How is quality inspected?
Can your organisation obtain foreign currency to buy machinery, spare parts or software licences?
questions.note: Over half of Ethiopian firms name access to finance as their principal obstacle. Separating FX for capital goods from FX for cloud services (A7) matters because they are rationed differently.

questions.text: How often do power interruptions stop production?
questions.note: Around 90% of Ethiopian firms reported outages in the FAT survey year. Automation raises the cost of an interruption, so this conditions what is worth deploying.

sections.title: Academia and research module
sections.help: For universities, research institutes, TVETs and schools. Every sector module follows the same shape so that sectors remain comparable.

questions.text: List the AI, data science or machine learning programmes you run.
questions.help: There is no public national inventory of Ethiopian AI programmes or their intakes. This item builds the first one.

fields.label: Are students actually graduating from it yet?

options.label: Not yet: first cohort still enrolled

questions.note: Announced intake and realised graduation diverge sharply in Ethiopian higher education: national PhD intake exceeded 5,000 while graduations remained in the hundreds. Asking both separates capacity from ambition.

questions.text: What share of academic staff in your computing or AI unit hold a PhD?
questions.note: Tests progress against the national 0:70:30 BSc:MSc:PhD staffing target, and provides the faculty-pipeline denominator for assessing whether a new AI university can be staffed without drawing from existing ones.

questions.text: In the last three years, how many academic staff have left your computing or AI unit?
questions.note: Current Ethiopian academic brain-drain figures do not exist; the numbers in circulation date from the 1990s and 2000s or are unsourced. This produces a contemporary measure.

questions.text: Where did they go?
How is AI research in your institution funded?

options.label: A mix of institutional and external funding
Mainly foreign donor or partner funding

questions.note: Tests the paper's claim that Ethiopia's strongest AI research capability is sustained by donors and external partners rather than by the state.

questions.text: Who do your researchers publish with?

options.label: Institutions in India, China, Korea or the Gulf
Institutions in Europe or North America

questions.note: Bibliometric evidence shows Ethiopian AI co-authorship dominated by India and South Korea rather than by the Western diaspora. This corroborates that from the respondent side and tests an assumption the paper previously made.

questions.text: When were your AI or data science course materials last substantially revised?
Do teachers at your school use AI tools for any of the following? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Grading or giving feedback on student work

questions.text: Have you noticed students using AI tools (like ChatGPT) to complete homework or exams?

options.label: Yes, it is a serious problem here
Not yet, but I expect it will happen

questions.text: Does your school have any guidance or policy for teachers or students on responsible AI use?

sections.title: Government and public service module
sections.help: For federal and regional government bodies and state-owned enterprises. Every sector module follows the same shape so that sectors remain comparable.

questions.text: For each area, what is your current status?

row_options.label: Citizen-facing chatbot, helpdesk or call-centre assistance
Digitising paper records (scanning, OCR, Ethiopic text extraction)
Tax, customs or revenue risk scoring
Translating official content into Ethiopian languages
Case triage, permit or licence processing

questions.note: The same status matrix as every other sector module, so government can be ranked against health, finance and agriculture rather than described alone.

questions.text: Through which channels do citizens actually reach this service?

options.label: In person at a woreda or branch office
Through kebele officials or local agents
A call centre or IVR line
Citizens do not interact with this service directly

questions.note: A government AI system reachable only through a web portal serves the roughly one-fifth of the population that is online. Measures the delivery surface, not the build.

questions.text: In how many languages is this service available to citizens?
questions.note: Constitutionally the working language question; operationally the exclusion question.

questions.text: Do you hold machine-readable administrative data (registers, case files, service records)?

options.label: Yes, and we share them with other bodies or publish them
Some, poorly organised or partly on paper

questions.text: Where a decision affecting a citizen is made or assisted by software, is there a stated legal basis and a route to challenge it?

options.label: Yes; both a published legal basis and a published route to challenge
A legal basis, but no published route to challenge
We make no automated or AI-assisted decisions about citizens

questions.note: The regulatory gate for this module. Proclamation 1321/2024 creates data-subject rights; this measures whether any machinery exists to exercise them.

questions.text: How is your AI or digital work funded, and when does the current funding end?

options.label: Donor or loan-financed project ending within two years
Donor or loan-financed project ending within one year

questions.note: Government digital programmes in Ethiopia are substantially loan- and donor-financed. Asked identically in every module so the dependency is comparable across sectors.

sections.title: National policy and coordination module
sections.help: For institutions that set, fund, regulate or coordinate AI rather than only use it. These questions are about the national picture, not about your own systems.
sections.note: Deliberately NOT built to the common sector-module shape. The other modules share a use-case matrix, a delivery channel and a language question so that sectors stay comparable with each other. This one is not a sector: forcing it into that shape would ask a policy body which channel its citizens reach its chatbot through, and learn nothing. It answers a different question and is reported separately.

questions.text: Which of these does your organisation actually do?
questions.help: Choose everything that applies in practice, not everything in the mandate.

options.label: Provide data or compute infrastructure to others

questions.note: 'In practice, not in the mandate' is doing the work here. The gap between the two is §4.2's concentration question measured from the inside, and it is the one thing a document review cannot establish.

questions.text: Which sectors does your organisation's AI work contribute to?
questions.help: Choose up to five.

questions.text: How would you describe the spread of AI adoption across Ethiopia today?

options.label: Widespread: most large organisations use AI in production
Established in a few sectors, rare elsewhere
I do not have a basis to judge

questions.note: The same judgement the study measures directly from 400 organisations. Comparing what the institutions responsible for AI believe is happening against what the organisational sample shows is a finding in itself, and it is the reason this question is asked of them rather than inferred.

questions.text: How much do you agree with each statement about the national picture?

rows.label: Responsibility for AI is clearly divided between institutions
Mandates overlap or conflict in practice
We can measure how much AI is actually being adopted
Funding is adequate for what the policy asks of us
The skills pipeline meets what the country needs
Organisations outside government are properly consulted
Regional states can act on AI, not only the federal level

questions.note: 'Mandates overlap' is asked straight rather than through an inference, and it is deliberately paired with 'responsibility is clearly divided': a respondent who agrees with both is telling us something the KII guide (Annex F) should follow up.

questions.text: Does your organisation measure AI adoption in Ethiopia or in your sector?
questions.note: A mandate to monitor adoption with no measurement behind it is the gap this study exists to fill, and the answer determines whether AI-MAP is duplicating work or supplying something missing.

questions.text: What most holds back AI adoption nationally? Choose up to five.

options.label: Data is missing, fragmented or on paper

questions.note: Deliberately overlaps K1, which asks organisations about their own barriers. Whether the institutions setting policy name the same constraints as the organisations living with them is a reportable divergence.

questions.text: What single change would most improve AI adoption in Ethiopia?
questions.help: Optional, and quoted anonymously if at all.

sections.title: Data availability and standardisation
sections.help: This section fills the white paper's data-asset register (§6).

questions.text: Does your organisation hold datasets that could be used to train or evaluate AI models?
Please describe your most significant datasets.

fields.label: Could it be shared for research?

options.label: Would need a decision above my level

questions.text: Which data management practices are in place? Tick all that apply.

options.label: A named data owner or steward
Documented consent basis for personal data

questions.text: Are you aware of the Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024?

options.label: Yes, and we have taken steps to comply
Yes, but no action taken yet

questions.text: Have you ever tried to obtain data from another Ethiopian organisation?

options.label: Yes, but we were refused or it never arrived

questions.text: What blocked it?

options.label: Data was not in a usable format
Quality was too poor to use

questions.note: Feeds §6.4 on data-sharing failure modes.

questions.text: Which of these standardisation problems affect your data? Tick all that apply.

options.label: Inconsistent Ethiopic text encoding or spelling variants
No standard address or location format
No unique identifier to link records across systems
Different code lists for the same thing across systems

questions.note: The calendar and Ethiopic-encoding items are Ethiopia-specific and are a novel contribution of this instrument.

questions.text: Would your organisation contribute data to a national, publicly governed data or language commons?

options.label: Yes, if there were clear legal protection
Only in return for access or payment

questions.text: Is your organisation's data stored inside Ethiopia, outside, or both?

sections.title: Infrastructure and compute
sections.help: This section produces the first national inventory of AI compute capacity.

questions.text: What computing resources does your organisation have access to?

options.label: At least one GPU suitable for machine learning
Colocation in a commercial data centre
Shared access via a university or partner

questions.text: Please list the GPUs or accelerators you have. This builds the national compute inventory.

options.label: Open to external researchers on request
Saturated: a constraint on our work

questions.text: Would your organisation be willing to share spare compute capacity through a federated national research pool?
questions.note: Directly tests the §7.2 'federate before you build' recommendation.

questions.text: What is the single biggest infrastructure constraint on doing more with AI?

options.label: Foreign currency to pay for cloud services
Nobody who can operate the infrastructure

constraints.message: That is more IT staff than the organisation has employees. Please check both answers.
constraints.note: The single most common inconsistency in organisational surveys: a respondent reads 'how many staff work in IT' as 'how many staff' and repeats the total. Caught while they are still on the question, it is a correction; caught in analysis, it is a dropped case.

constraints.message: More pilots reached production than were started. Please check both numbers.
constraints.note: Feeds pilot_conversion, which is a headline indicator. Unchecked, D7b > D7 publishes a conversion rate above 100%.

constraints.message: Please give a four-digit year that is not in the future.
constraints.note: The upper bound is computed at render time, not stored: a fixed year silently starts rejecting valid answers on 1 January. The floor is 1850 rather than something recent because Ethiopian institutions are old -- Ethio Telecom dates from 1894, Addis Ababa University from 1950, the National Bank from 1963 -- and a 20th-century floor would reject exactly the largest organisations in the frame.

constraints.message: Your head office region is not among the regions you operate in.
constraints.note: Flagged, never blocked. It is usually an oversight, but a holding company registered in one region with no operations there is a real arrangement, and refusing to accept it would fabricate a correction rather than record a fact.

constraints.message: You said earlier that your organisation has never used AI. Please check that answer, or choose a different option here.
constraints.note: D15 is deliberately asked of everyone, not only adopters -- the global pattern is agent adoption outrunning the governance that should precede it, and routing it away from non-adopters would hide exactly that. So the ITEM stays universal and only the contradictory ANSWER is blocked.

constraints.message: A production system is reported, but the organisation was recorded as never having used AI.
constraints.note: Flagged rather than blocked because D5 is a checklist and the respondent may be correcting their earlier answer by ticking it. The pair is the definitional gate doing its job: the organisation has something it does not consider AI.

constraints.message: Case triage is reported in production, but the organisation reports making no automated decisions about citizens.
constraints.note: Never blocked. A triage system that ranks a queue without deciding an outcome is a real and defensible distinction, and the respondent knows their system better than the form does. But under Proclamation 1321/2024 the gap between the two answers is exactly where a data-subject right goes unhonoured, so it is recorded.

constraints.message: At least one sensitive use is reported with no review process, alongside a view that current safeguards are enough.
constraints.note: Never blocked: the respondent may hold both views consistently (e.g. 'no formal process, but nothing has gone wrong'). Flagged because the combination is exactly what an ethics section exists to surface -- oversight and the belief that oversight is unnecessary, stated in the same response.
